metaDescription: Six electric fireplace heaters for RVs compared: built-in RV models, a wall-mount curved unit and portable stove-style heaters, with wattage and install notes.
expertTake: The Furrion 30 inch RV fireplace is the best pick for owners who want a built-in look with real heat, and the duraflame portable is the value pick for a rig with no wall to cut. Anyone who cares only about warmth per amp should skip fireplaces and buy a plain ceramic heater.
introParagraphs: An electric fireplace is a resistance heater in decorative clothing. Behind the glass sits a standard element and fan, and the flame is an LED effect that has nothing to do with the heat. You get the look of a hearth without a flue, fuel or open flame.

In an RV that trade makes sense for living areas where atmosphere counts. The question is the format: a built-in unit that lives in the wall, a wall-mount panel, or a portable stove that sits on the floor and goes into storage for summer.

products.name: Furrion 30 Inch RV Electric Fireplace FF30SC15A-BL
products.description:
Furrion builds this fireplace for RV use, with a 30 inch width, an adjustable temperature range and proximity sensors that shut it off when objects come too close. The listing claims it can heat up to 500 square feet, which is generous for a 1500 watt class heater, so read it as a supplemental zone heater for the living area. The multicolor flame is a decorative LED effect.

Proximity sensing is the feature that makes it feel RV-minded, because cabins are tight and curtains and cushions end up close to everything. Next to the portable units in this roundup, it is fixed in the wall and carries no tip-over risk. That permanence also means a real installation job.

Plan the cut-out and the power run before buying, and confirm the unit fits between studs. Keep the front glass clean with a dry microfiber cloth. If your RV already has a Furrion appliance line, parts and support are easier to find. The wall behind a built-in often hides water lines or wiring, so open it carefully, and use a dedicated outlet so the unit never shares a circuit with the microwave.
products.bestFor: Living areas where you want a built-in look with automatic safety sensing.
pros: Built for RV installation at 30 inches wide
Proximity sensors shut it off when objects get close
Fixed mount cannot tip over on the road
cons: Needs a wall cut-out and a power run
Coverage claim is generous for the wattage

products.name: CONTOURE 31 Inch Built-In RV Electric Fireplace with Remote
products.description:
CONTOURE offers a 31 inch built-in RV fireplace with a remote and a wide 62 to 82 degree Fahrenheit thermostat range. The maker positions it as supplemental zone heating, an honest description for a fireplace heater. Multi-colored flames and crystal colors let you tune the mood.

Its extra inch of width over the Furrion hardly matters; the decision comes down to cutout dimensions and features. The wider temperature range gives more control, and the remote is useful when the unit sits high in a wall. Against the Greystone curved unit, it has a more conventional flat front.

Measure the opening twice before ordering, since a built-in has no flexibility. Keep a clearance around it per the maker's instructions. Dust the vents with a brush each season. Since the front of a built-in sits close to seating, ask yourself where the cushions end up when the dinette is converted to a bed, and keep the clearance the maker specifies even then.
products.bestFor: Owners who want a wide built-in with a remote and a broad temperature range.
pros: 31 inch width fills a larger wall space
cons: Little detail on wattage in the listing

products.name: Greystone 26 Inch Curved Electric Fireplace with Remote and Trim Kit
products.description:
Greystone's 26 inch unit has a curved glass front, seven temperature settings and nine LED flame gradients, with a remote and a trim kit in the box. The curved front gives a contemporary look and a slightly smaller footprint than the 30 inch RV units. A trim kit simplifies the finish around the cut-out.

Seven temperature settings give finer control than a simple high and low. This is a residential-style electric fireplace, not an RV-certified unit, so check that the supply and mounting suit your rig. Beside the Furrion, it lacks RV-specific sensors but costs less.

Curved glass shows fingerprints, so keep a microfiber cloth handy. Test the fit in the cutout before fastening. Check the plug and receptacle for a snug connection. A fireplace that plugs into a wall outlet is only as safe as that outlet, so replace a loose receptacle before the first cold night rather than after.
products.bestFor: A modern, compact wall fireplace with fine temperature steps.
pros: Seven temperature settings for fine control
cons: No proximity sensing in the listing

products.name: RealSmart 22 Inch Freestanding Infrared Fireplace Heater
products.description:
RealSmart sells a 22 inch freestanding fireplace stove with three infrared quartz tubes and 5,118 BTU output. It stands 21.65 inches tall and weighs 10.47 pounds, light enough to move between rooms and stow for summer. A three-sided window gives the 3D flame effect.

Infrared quartz heat warms people and surfaces directly, so it suits a seating area better than a closed room. Unlike a built-in, it needs no installation, which is a big advantage for renters and weekenders. Set against the Shinic mini, it is larger and heavier, but the flame display is more convincing.

Secure it in a corner with a strap when traveling. Quartz tubes are fragile, so pad the unit with a blanket and wedge it upright in a closet. A cracked tube is a reason to stop using it. Keep fabrics away from the front, and remember that radiant warmth can scorch a cushion left directly in line with the tubes. A corner placement with a clear arc in front is the safest arrangement in a small rig.
products.bestFor: Renters and weekenders who want a no-install fireplace with infrared warmth.
pros: Three quartz tubes give radiant warmth
cons: Quartz tubes can crack in transit
Radiant heat leaves the far end cooler

products.name: duraflame Electric Fireplace Portable Space Heater 750W/1500W

specList.label: Flame
specList.value: Glowing log set and ember bed

products.description:
duraflame's portable fireplace offers 750 and 1500 watt settings and a glowing log set with an ember bed. The maker quotes 4,600 BTU and positions it as supplemental zone heating for up to 400 square feet. Its 750 watt step is the helpful one for RVs, drawing about 6.3 amps.

It is a recognized brand in decorative fireplaces, which brings a service network and easier access to replacement remotes and logs if a part fails. Versus the built-ins, it needs no install and can be stored in a closet. The trade is that it takes floor space and tips more easily than a fixed unit.

Strap it down for travel and never run it while driving. Dust the vents each month, and run the fan for a minute after turning the heat off so the element cools evenly. Keep curtains well away from the front, and tuck the cord along the wall so nobody steps on it. Owners often leave the flame effect running by itself in the evening, which costs almost nothing and gives the cabin its mood.
products.bestFor: A low-cost, no-install fireplace with two power steps.
pros: Glowing log set and ember bed look good

products.name: Shinic Portable Electric Fireplace Heater 1500W/750W with 3D Flame
products.description:
Shinic builds a small fireplace-style heater around a PTC ceramic element with 1500 and 750 watt settings and a 3D flame effect. The maker claims warmth in about three seconds and quotes 5,118 BTU, which is just the standard output for 1500 watts. V0 flame-retardant plastics cover the housing, and a leather carry handle makes it easy to move.

It is the most compact option here, so it suits a bunk room or a small seating nook better than a full living area. Next to the RealSmart, it is smaller and lighter and uses a fan with ceramic rather than infrared tubes. The flame effect makes it feel like a fireplace even on a small scale.

Stow it in a drawer for travel. Wipe the vents when cool. Use the 750 watt step to share a circuit. It is a sensible nightstand or bunk-end heater that happens to look good, and it moves easily when you want the warmth somewhere else.
products.bestFor: Small spaces that want a fireplace look on a tight budget.
cons: Too small for a large living area

buyingCriteria.explanation: In an electric fireplace the flames are LEDs and the warmth comes from a resistance element. A 1500 watt unit makes about 5,100 BTU whatever the flame looks like, which is why duraflame quotes 4,600 BTU and Shinic 5,118. Do not pay extra for flame effects if heat is the goal; a plain ceramic unit gives you the same warmth for less.

Built-in units like the Furrion, CONTOURE and Greystone sit in the wall and cannot tip. Freestanding stoves like the RealSmart and duraflame need no install and store away. Pick based on whether you want a permanent living area feature. Many owners who start with a portable stove end up cutting in a built-in after a second winter, so buy the portable first only if you are unsure.

A built-in needs an exact opening, and RV walls are thin with studs and wiring behind them. Measure the width, height and depth twice, and check the wall thickness, because RV walls are often thinner than a residential insert expects. The Furrion is 30 inches, the CONTOURE 31 and the Greystone 26.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Amp draw on a 30 amp service
buyingCriteria.explanation: A 1500 watt fireplace draws about 12.5 amps and a 750 watt step about 6.3. On a shared 30 amp circuit, run the lower step with an air conditioner. Plan your loads before you plug in, and remember that the water heater element and converter share the same service.

The Furrion adds proximity sensors that shut it off when something sits too close. In a tight RV with curtains and cushions, that automatic shutoff is a real advantage, though it never replaces keeping the area clear. Portable units rely on tip-over and overheat protection.

Listings claim 400 to 500 square feet, but 1500 watts suits about 150 square feet at the usual 10 watts per square foot. Use fireplaces as zone heaters in a living area, and let the furnace or a ceramic unit handle the rest of the rig.

specDecoder.meaning: BTU measures heat per hour. Any 1500 watt resistance heater produces about 5,100 BTU.
specDecoder.watchFor: RealSmart and Shinic quote 5,118, and duraflame quotes 4,600.

specDecoder.meaning: The range is the set of temperatures the unit can hold. A wide range gives more control.
specDecoder.watchFor: Furrion lists 65F to 80F and CONTOURE lists 62F to 82F.

specDecoder.meaning: A proximity sensor detects objects near the unit and shuts it off. It prevents scorching of curtains and cushions, which matters most in a small cabin where soft furnishings sit close to everything.
specDecoder.watchFor: Only the Furrion lists proximity sensors here.

specDecoder.meaning: Quartz tubes radiate warmth directly to people and surfaces. They do not warm the air quickly.
Coverage is a marketing estimate for a specific insulation level. Practical coverage is roughly 10 watts per square foot.
specDecoder.watchFor: Furrion claims up to 500 sq ft, and duraflame claims 400.

howWeEvaluated.title: RV suitability
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated RV-specific fireplaces from residential models and judged each on fit for a moving rig. The Furrion and CONTOURE are built for RVs, while the others are residential units. This follows the listing text.

howWeEvaluated.title: Heat output
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared BTU claims and wattage steps against what 1500 watts can really produce. Claims above about 5,100 BTU were treated as marketing. We credited the 750 watt steps for shared circuits.

howWeEvaluated.title: Installation effort
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at cut-outs, mounting and power runs. Freestanding units scored highest for ease, and built-ins scored for permanence. Trim kits and remotes counted toward convenience.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety features
howWeEvaluated.description: We confirmed overheat, tip-over and proximity features in each listing. The Furrion's proximity sensing stands out. Where a listing was silent, no credit was given.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered recurring themes such as fan noise, flame brightness and remote reliability. Newer listings with limited history were treated cautiously, and we gave no credit for features a listing did not state. Conclusions rest on spec sheets, not bench work.

rows: Permanent wall feature in the living area

cards.label: Built-in
cards.text: The Furrion, CONTOURE and Greystone sit in the wall, take no floor space and cannot tip. They need cutting, wiring and exact measurements.

cards.label: Portable
cards.text: The RealSmart, duraflame and Shinic sit on the floor and store away. They are flexible but take space and need securing for travel.

howToChoose.note: Full-timers benefit from built-ins, and weekenders usually prefer portable.

howToChoose.subheading: For Ambience on a Budget Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Choose a unit whose flame effect and log set please you, and treat the heating as a bonus. Confirm tip-over protection and keep curtains clear.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The duraflame glowing log set and the RealSmart three-sided view offer the most convincing flames without installation.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You live in the RV and want a permanent feature. The Furrion repays its cost through RV-specific sensing and fit.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You camp occasionally. The Shinic or duraflame gives the look and some warmth.

maintenance.why: Dust restricts airflow and triggers odd smells. A brush clears it in under a minute, and the same pass lets you spot a loose connector or a frayed cord.
Fingerprints dull the flame effect. A dry microfiber cloth works best.
A warm plug indicates a poor connection. Replace the unit if it discolors.
Vibration loosens screws and trim. Tighten them before travel, especially on trim kits that rely on small screws or clips.
Weak cells cause missed commands. Keep a spare set.

faq.q: Does an electric fireplace heat as well as a normal heater?
faq.a: At the same wattage, yes. The element produces the same BTU, and the flame effect adds none. Fireplaces cost more for the look, so buy one because you like the look, not because you expect better heating.

faq.q: Can I run the flame without heat?
faq.a: Most units allow flame-only mode, which uses very little power. Check the manual for your model. Flame-only mode is a good way to keep the cabin looking warm in shoulder season without drawing real power.

faq.q: How many amps does it draw?
faq.a: A 1500 watt unit draws about 12.5 amps and a 750 watt step about 6.3. Plan your loads on a 30 amp service.

faq.q: Is a built-in fireplace worth the install?
faq.a: For full-timers yes, because it frees floor space and cannot tip. Weekenders usually prefer a portable stove, which also leaves the wall intact when you sell the rig.
No. Electric fireplaces have no combustion, so they need no flue or exhaust.

faq.q: Can I use a residential fireplace in an RV?
faq.a: It can work if the supply and mounting suit your rig. RV-specific units add proximity sensing and fit RV walls.
